title: Architecture and business foundations
task_statement: Turn cost, capacity, and quality requirements into numbers that a design can meet. (Inference: task wording from repo lesson 7-4A, not from the exam guide)

components.name: Token cost model
components.first_principle: Each token class has its own price, so the cost of a request is the sum of its classes.

nodes.label: Price per million tokens by class

steps: The API reports token counts for each class in the usage fields.
Cache writes and cache reads have their own multiplier on the base input price.
Thinking tokens bill as output tokens.
Batch requests cost 50 percent less than standard requests.
Multiply each count by its rate and divide the result by one million.
Multiply the cost per request by the daily request volume and the number of days.
Compare the monthly figure with the spend cap before launch.
pros: The arithmetic gives an exact figure once the token counts are known.
The cost of a request is visible before any load test runs.
Usage fields show the split between cached and uncached tokens.
cons: Token counts change with the tokenizer, so a sample of real requests gives the best estimate.
Prices differ by model, endpoint, and platform.
Prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more on Claude Haiku 5.5.
use_when: A design choice changes the token count per request or the request volume.
A budget owner must approve a monthly spend figure.
do_not_use_when: The work has no token cost, such as a local function with no model call.
The price for the chosen platform is unknown. Look up the platform price first.

constraints.choice: Forecast cost at peak request volume, not at the monthly average.
Sum the usage fields for each request each day.
constraints.combination: Alert when the daily total passes the forecast. (Inference)

components.name: Spend caps and usage tiers
components.first_principle: A spend cap stops usage at a set monthly amount, so it limits the worst-case bill.
steps: The organization sits in a usage tier with a monthly spend cap.
Each workspace can set a lower spend limit in the Console.
Rate limits apply per model class in requests and tokens per minute.
When usage reaches a spend limit you set, requests return HTTP 400.
When usage reaches the tier cap, requests return HTTP 429 without a retry-after header.
Raise or remove the limit to restore access sooner.
pros: A cap bounds the monthly loss from a runaway loop.
Workspace limits separate budgets for teams and environments.
A tier move raises the rate limits and the spend cap together.
cons: A tier cap returns 429, which looks like a rate limit, but retries fail until access resumes.
Spend on Claude Platform on AWS can take about 2 hours to show, so usage can pass a cap before requests stop.
The Default Workspace cannot have a spend limit.
use_when: A team or environment needs its own monthly budget.
A new workload must not exceed a fixed monthly amount.
do_not_use_when: The goal is faster throughput. Rate limits control request speed, not the budget.
A usage report is the only goal. A report alone does not stop usage.

components.exam_tie: F1. Expect a scenario with a shared key and a budget owner. The credited answer scopes the budget at the workspace level. (Inference)
components.trap: A retry loop for every 429 looks right. A spend cap 429 has no retry-after header, so retries fail until access resumes.
components.decision_rule: Use a workspace spend limit for budget control and a rate limit change for throughput.
components.exam_tip: A 429 with no retry-after header points to a spend cap, not to a rate limit.

components.name: Acceptance thresholds for model output
components.first_principle: Each quality adjective needs a metric, a threshold, and an owner before the build starts. (Inference)
steps: Write the requirement as one sentence that names the quality.
Name a metric that measures that quality on a fixed evaluation set.
Set a numeric threshold that the metric must meet.
Name one owner who signs off the threshold.
Run the same evaluation before each release.
Review the threshold when the traffic or the task changes.
pros: A number gives all builders the same target.
A threshold makes a release decision testable.
An owner answers for the number.
cons: A threshold chosen without data can be wrong.
A green metric can hide a user problem when traffic changes.
A fixed evaluation set can drift from live traffic.
use_when: An output error has a cost, such as a wrong date in a legal form.
Two or more teams hand off work that depends on the quality claim.
do_not_use_when: A one-person demo has no users and no money at stake.
The output has no quality claim that a test can check.

constraints.choice: Name one owner for each threshold.
constraints.combination: Review the owner sign-off on a fixed date.

constraints.choice: Run the same evaluation before each release.
constraints.combination: Add a sample of live traffic when the fixed set no longer matches users. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Measure the cost of a wrong output before setting the threshold.
constraints.combination: Lower the threshold only when an error costs little. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Write each metric in the terms that the task owner uses.

components.exam_tie: F1. Expect an option with a vague quality word and an option with a metric and a threshold. The credited answer names both. (Inference)
components.trap: Launch first and tune the threshold later sounds agile, but users meet the errors before any bar exists.
components.decision_rule: Attach a metric, a threshold, and an owner to each quality word before the build starts.
components.exam_tip: If the stem says fast or accurate with no number, the answer adds a metric and a threshold.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{Budget or throughput problem?} -->|Budget| B[Workspace spend limit]
  A -->|Throughput| C[Rate limit change or retry]
  B --> D{Forecast above tier cap?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Move tier or cut tokens]
  D -->|No| F[Set alert threshold]
  C --> G{429 has retry-after?}
  G -->|Yes| H[Wait and retry]
  G -->|No| I[Check tier spend cap]
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  T[Token classes] --> R[Rate per class]
  R --> C[Cost per request]
  C --> F[Daily volume]
  F --> M[Monthly forecast]
  M --> K{Under spend cap?}
  K -->|No| X[Move tier or cut tokens]
  K -->|Yes| W[Workspace limit]
  W --> A[Alert threshold]
